Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Corporation ------- Plaintiff
Vs
MV Helal Kamal and others ------- Defendants

4. The legal position is that when an Act is repealed any delegated legislation made under the Act falls to the ground with the statute unless it is expressly preserved. See Watson vs Winch (1916)1 KB 688. On a scrutiny of the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978, it is found that the Original Side Rules framed by the Calcutta High Court under clause 37 of Letters Patent, 1865 have not been preserved by the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978. Thus the Original Side Rules died its natural death with the promulgation of Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978. Therefore, there can be no manner of recourse to the Original Side Rules in any matter now. 

 5. Let us now examine the legal status of the Admiralty court. The Admiralty jurisdiction was conferred on this Court by clause 26 of the Charter of 1774 i.e. by that clause power was given to the Supreme Court of Bengal to hear, examine, try and determine all causes, civil and maritime and all pleas of contracts" and "all matters and contracts which in any manner whatsoever relate to freight or money due for ship hired and let out, transport-money, maritime usury or bottomery or to extortions, injuries, complaints, demands, and matters, civil and maritime, whatsoever, between merchants, owners, proprietors of ships and vessels, employed or used within the jurisdiction or between others contracted, done, had or commenced, in, upon or by the sea, or public rivers, or ports." This clause described the Admiralty jurisdiction of the Supreme Court as the same as used and exercised in that part of Great Britain called "England" together with all and singular incidents, emergents and dependencies annexed". This jurisdiction was continued by clause 31 of Letters Patent of 1862 and clause 32 of the Letters Patent of 1865. 

 6. In England High Court used to exercise Admiralty jurisdiction under the Admiralty Act of 1861. But in order to bring about uniformity between the jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty in England and the Admiralty jurisdiction of High Courts in British possessions the Parliament enacted the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890. Pursuant to that Act the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) 1891 was passed declaring certain Courts including the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal as the Colonial Court of Admiralty so as to enable them to exercise the same jurisdiction as that of the High Court of England as existing in 1890. In 1890 the Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court of England was used to be exercised under the Admiralty Act of 1861 of the British Parliament which became the basis of the Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court of Calcutta. The said jurisdiction was preserved by section 106 of the Government of India Act, 1915 and section 223 of the Government of India Act, 1935. In 1947 after partition of India in exercise of the power conferred by section 9 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the High Court (Bengal) Order, 1947 was passed by which the Admiralty Jurisdiction was conferred upon the High Court of East Bengal. 

 7. Now let us see what is the nature of the jurisdiction exercised by this Court under a statute of parliament. This question came up for consideration in the case of Dhaka Jute Mills Ltd (19 DLR 735) before the Dacca High Court in 1967 where it was observed that matters decided under the Companies Act in the High Court by a Single Judge are not disposed of in exercise of its Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction which has not yet exercised such jurisdiction. Cases under the Companies Act are decided by way of a Special Statutory Jurisdiction conferred upon the Court by the Act itself and it would be a misnomer to describe such jurisdiction as Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction. 

 8. In the case of Saleh Steel Industries Ltd 35 DLR (AD) 188 the same question came up for consideration before the Appellate Division. It appears that the majority did not advert to the nature of duty exercised by the Admiralty Court i.e. whether it exercises Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction, or Extraordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction or Special Statutory Jurisdiction. However, the minority view correctly addressed to the issue. His Lordship observed that Admiralty Jurisdiction is completely different from both Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction and Extraordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction of the High Court. Original Part IX of the Code of Civil Procedure contained special provisions relating to the Chartered High Courts. Similarly, Original section 116 provided that Part IX applied to Chartered High Courts. Original section 117 also provided that save as provided in this part or in Part X or in Rules, the provisions of this Code shall apply to such High Courts. Thus section 117 applied the provisions of the Code to Chartered High Courts in the exercise of their Appellate Civil Jurisdiction including their jurisdiction in Letters Patent Appeals. Unfortunately, neither 19 DLR nor 26 DLR 19 were referred to in 35 DLR case. Thus, though it was observed that the Admiralty, jurisdiction is neither Ordinary Original Civil jurisdiction nor Extraordinary Original Civil jurisdiction of the High Court yet it was not said what kind of jurisdiction it is. It brooks no controversy that the Admiralty jurisdiction is special statutory jurisdiction as it emanates from a statute. 

 10. The drawing up of a decree is nothing but a procedural matter and procedure is provided to augment the interest of justice and not to deny justice to a party. It must be remembered that the Court exists for dispensation of justice and in doing so the court is competent to exercise its discretion in the background of the case. The proceedings initiated before the Admiralty Court is undoubtedly civil proceedings and there is nothing in the Admiralty Act or the Rules to preclude the Admiralty Court from exercising the power, which inheres in every court of plenary jurisdiction to prevent miscarriage of justice. A similar question came up for consideration before the Appellate Division in the Moni Begum's case reported in 46 DLR (AD) 154. The Appellate Division while considering the question of application of the provision of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the proceedings in Writ in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution observed that the provision of section 141 of the Code does not in terms apply to proceedings in Writ in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. But the Court, in its discretion, can apply the principles as distinguished from the technical provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to meet the exigencies of the situation in appropriate cases on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience. In what situation the principles of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applied and to what extent may perhaps, be left to the wise discretion of the court itself. In other words, barring what is specifically provided for in the rules themselves the court is the master of its own procedure and it will exercise both its procedural and substantive discretions only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience. Thus it is now well settled that technicality of law cannot stand in the way of aggrieved party, more so when our Courts are not common law courts. Therefore, the legal position is that neither the Original Side Rules nor the Code applies to a proceeding in Admiralty Court. Strictly speaking, though the provisions of the Code, in its turn, do not apply to the Admiralty proceedings but in an appropriate case the court can apply the principle as distinguished from the technical provisions of the Code to meet the exigencies of the situation on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience. Besides, this court can always invoke its inherent jurisdiction to remedy a wrong. This Court is invested with wide powers to make such order in a case as it thought fit. The legal principle that every Court has inherent power to act ex-debitio justiciae to do that real and substantial justice for which alone the court exists or to prevent abuse of the process of the court. The courts are to act upon the principles that every procedure further the cause of justice is to be understood as permissible till it is shown to be prohibited by the law. The inherent powers of the Court are such as are used to secure the ends of justice or to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court. The Court cannot turn its blind eye to a situation which causes injustice to a party. There cannot be an injury without a remedy. In the light of the aforesaid principles let us deal with the instant case. The petitioner was prevented by sufficient cause in filing the requisite within a reasonable time. Since there is no time limit now for filing of requisite for drawing up of a decree in the Admiralty suit, the decree holder must come within a reasonable time unless prevented by sufficient cause. In the instant case, the petitioner satisfactorily explained the delay. Hence I am inclined to allow the application, as the Court is the master of its own procedure.
